title: Implement optical flow method
aim: To estimate the apparent motion of image points between consecutive video frames with sparse (Lucas-Kanade) and dense (Farneback, DIS) optical flow, and to check the Lucas-Kanade solution against an implementation written from scratch.
objectives: Track Shi-Tomasi corners through a video with pyramidal Lucas-Kanade and draw their tracks.
Compute dense Farneback and DIS optical flow and show it as a colour-wheel image and a vector field.
Solve the Lucas-Kanade least-squares problem in NumPy and compare the answer with OpenCV.
theory: Optical flow is the 2D vector field $(u, v)$ of the apparent motion of each pixel between consecutive frames. Assuming constant brightness, a first-order Taylor expansion gives the flow constraint, one equation in two unknowns (aperture problem):
$$I(x, y, t) = I(x + u, y + v, t + 1) \quad \Rightarrow \quad I_x u + I_y v + I_t = 0$$

Lucas-Kanade assumes constant flow inside a small window ($21 \times 21$ pixels here). Stacking the window's constraints gives $A \mathbf{v} = -\mathbf{b}$ with $A = [I_x \; I_y]$ and $\mathbf{b} = I_t$, solved by least squares. $A^T A$ is the structure tensor, well conditioned only at corners, so tracking starts from Shi-Tomasi corners; a pyramid handles large motions.
$$\mathbf{v} = \begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \end{bmatrix} = (A^T A)^{-1} A^T (-\mathbf{b}), \qquad A^T A = \begin{bmatrix} \sum I_x^2 & \sum I_x I_y \\ \sum I_x I_y & \sum I_y^2 \end{bmatrix}$$

Dense methods return a vector at every pixel. Farneback fits a quadratic polynomial to each neighbourhood; DIS matches patches on a coarse grid and refines variationally, several times faster. The field is shown as a quiver plot or an HSV image (hue $=$ direction, brightness $=$ magnitude).
tools: Python 3.11, OpenCV 5.0 (calcOpticalFlowPyrLK, goodFeaturesToTrack, calcOpticalFlowFarneback, DISOpticalFlow), NumPy, Matplotlib
dataset: OpenCV sample videos vtest.avi (static surveillance camera, 768 x 576, 10 fps, walking pedestrians) and Megamind.avi (animation clip, 720 x 528) from the OpenCV samples/data repository.
algorithm: Read the first 61 frames of vtest.avi in grayscale and detect up to 400 Shi-Tomasi corners in frame 0.
Track the corners with cv2.calcOpticalFlowPyrLK ($21 \times 21$ window, 3 levels) and draw the tracks of points that move more than 0.5 px.
Every 15 frames save a snapshot and re-detect corners in regions that have none.
Compute Farneback and DIS (medium) flow on 20 consecutive frame pairs and record the run time and flow magnitudes.
Show the flow as an HSV colour-wheel image and a 16 px quiver plot, then repeat on a Megamind.avi pair.
Solve Lucas-Kanade in NumPy from the normal equations $A^T A \mathbf{v} = -A^T I_t$ with iterative refinement.
Run OpenCV single-level LK on the same ten corners and compare the two results.

figures.caption: Figure 9.1: Sparse Lucas-Kanade tracks on vtest.avi at frames 15, 30, 45 and 60. Coloured lines are the paths of moving corners.
Figure 9.2: Farneback flow between frames 100 and 101 of vtest.avi: input, HSV colour-wheel image and flow vectors magnified four times.
Figure 9.3: Farneback (left) and DIS medium (right) flow for the same pair, with run time per frame.
Figure 9.4: Farneback flow on Megamind.avi frames 121 to 122. The moving head gets one hue and the quiver plot shows its vectors.
Figure 9.5: NumPy Lucas-Kanade (red) and OpenCV single-level LK (cyan) on ten corners, arrows magnified six times.

results: Sparse LK kept all 400 initial corners. With re-detection the count grew to 1078 by frame 60, an average of 802.8 per frame. About 102 points per frame moved more than 0.5 px, with a mean displacement of 5.55 px; these are the pedestrians. Over all points the mean displacement was 0.74 px.

On 20 pairs of $768 \times 576$ frames Farneback took 180.0 ms per frame (mean 0.231 px, max 13.74 px). DIS took 53.3 ms (mean 0.169 px, max 12.46 px) and left a cleaner background. On the Megamind pair the mean flow was 0.64 px and the maximum 10.30 px.

The NumPy Lucas-Kanade solver agreed with OpenCV on all ten points. On a walking person both gave $(3.70, -2.10)$ px and on the static lamp post $(-0.01, 0.00)$ px. The mean absolute difference was 0.002 px.
conclusion: Sparse Lucas-Kanade tracking recovers sub-pixel motion at textured corners, and both dense methods separate the walking people from the static background, DIS about three times faster than Farneback. The least-squares LK solution written by hand reproduced OpenCV to within 0.002 px.
